title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Recall bid collapses in one township while zoning battles and power demands heat up statewide.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're diving into a recall effort that just fell apart, keeping a big 500-acre project moving forward even as communities keep pushing back on power, water, and taxes.
That sounds like the latest chapter in a story we've been tracking for weeks now.
Exactly. A Michigan clerk rejected the petitions aimed at recalling the local officials who approved the rezoning.
So the project stays on track for now.
Right, and residents who opposed it are facing a tougher road if they want another vote.
This is the one in a community already split over how much electricity it will pull and what kind of tax breaks the company is getting.
We've seen this pattern before with these big facilities.
Yeah, developers come in promising jobs, but the trade-offs on the grid and local resources keep coming up.
The history here goes back months in several townships where rezoning fights turned into recall attempts or moratoriums.
How many places have tried something like this recall route?
A handful, but most of the pushback has been through zoning changes or temporary freezes instead.
That makes sense. Recalls are a heavy lift.
They are. And when they fail like this one did today, it signals the project is likely staying put.
What does that mean for the electric bills people are already worried about?
DTE is already asking regulators for two new gas plants because data centers are driving up demand across southeast Michigan.
Those plants would add to the load if they get built.
And older coal units are retiring at the same time, so the math could mean higher rates for everyone from Detroit out to Ann Arbor.
Water use is another big piece, right?
Cooling these facilities takes a lot, and that's why several townships are rewriting rules or extending bans to study the impact.
Farmland and rural towns are feeling it too.
The 500-acre footprint alone can change the character of a place, and the tax shifts can hit homeowners even if they're not right next door.
So who are the main players in this particular fight?
Local officials who approved the rezoning are still in place after the recall failed, the developer pushing the project, and the residents who gathered the petitions.
And now the clerk's decision keeps everything moving.
It does. The next steps could involve more legal challenges or just watching how the construction phase plays out.
What happens next on the bigger statewide level?
We have township leaders endorsing bills that would make data centers pay more for grid upgrades, which could ease some of the bill pressure if they pass.
That sounds like a direct response to the power hunger we're seeing.
It is, and it shows the resistance is spreading beyond just one community.
Any sense of how long these fights usually drag on?
Some moratoriums are already extended into early 2027, so we're looking at months more of studies and rule changes.
That gives residents time but also keeps uncertainty high for everyone.
Exactly. The big story here is that even when a recall fails, the underlying concerns about costs and resources are not going away.
We'll keep watching how other communities handle similar projects.
Now let's move to the quick hits from the last couple of days.
Yesterday in Saline Township the data center proposal kept advancing even after officials tightened zoning rules under pressure.
It could mean thousands of construction jobs, but the power and water demands are still a concern for people 30 miles away who might see higher utility rates.
Also yesterday, two more Metro Detroit suburbs changed their zoning codes after residents raised alarms about noise, water, and power strain.
Those changes could slow or block projects developers have been eyeing in the region.
Wixom is facing a lawsuit from a data center firm after the city blocked the plans.
The developer claims the zoning decisions killed the project unfairly, and taxpayers could end up covering legal costs.
On Thursday Solon Township extended its data center freeze another six months while they update rules on noise, traffic, and utility costs.
A West Michigan community did the same, pushing its moratorium out to at least early 2027.
That gives residents more time to look at the grid impacts and potential bill increases.
Wednesday brought news that Gaines Township will do decibel readings at a proposed site to see how much noise residents would hear from cooling fans and generators.
If it exceeds limits, that could reshape or stop the project.
Also on Wednesday, Michigan supervisors backed state bills that would force data centers to pay more toward grid upgrades.
Residents might see lower bills if those pass and local governments keep some control.
And Garfield Township voted to halt new proposals for a year while they study power, water, and noise limits in Grand Traverse County.
That pause prevents developers from filing before new restrictions are in place.
A lot of activity this week across the state.
It really shows how widespread these concerns have become.
Now for on deck.
No major public meetings listed for tonight or tomorrow that we've confirmed yet.
We'll keep an eye on any last-minute agendas that pop up and bring them to you tomorrow.
Listeners can always check the tracker for updates.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Recall Fails, But Data Center Fights Rage On Across Michigan
